set.d: radiocarbon-dated 1260–1390 (1988); first documented c. 1354; venerated by tradition as Christ's burial cloth
set.l: Turin Cathedral (Cathedral of St John the Baptist), Turin, Italy
set.m: Linen, three-to-one herringbone twill; image of undetermined origin

summary: A length of linen about 4.4 metres long bearing the faint, straw-coloured front and back image of a bearded man laid out in death, with reddish stains corresponding to the wounds of scourging, crowning with thorns, crucifixion and the lance. This full-length photograph also shows the scorch lines and triangular patches left by the fire of 1532. Venerated for centuries as the cloth in which Christ was buried, the Shroud is first documented at Lirey in France in the 1350s; in 1988 three laboratories radiocarbon-dated a sample of the linen to AD 1260–1390. The Catholic Church neither affirms nor denies its authenticity, while its popes have commended it to the faithful as an image that invites contemplation of the Passion.
facts: Independent radiocarbon tests carried out in 1988 by laboratories in Oxford, Tucson (University of Arizona) and Zurich (ETH) dated the sampled corner of the cloth, with 95% confidence, to AD 1260–1390 — a result accepted as valid by most experts, though contested by defenders of the cloth's authenticity.

In 1532 molten silver from its reliquary burned through the folded cloth at Chambéry; Poor Clare nuns sewed patches over the holes, which give the Shroud the symmetrical pattern of triangles seen here.

Pope John Paul II said in 1998 that because the question is not a matter of faith, the Church has no specific competence to pronounce on it and entrusts the investigation to scientists; in 2013 Pope Francis called it the 'icon of a man scourged and crucified'.
notes: Sorting year is the midpoint of the 1988 radiocarbon range (1260–1390). The Commons file credits the photograph to Giuseppe Enrie (1931), but this sepia, full-length positive with the pre-2002 patches may be a later reproduction or tinted version; the photographer attribution is unverified, so the old 'a' value (which named the photographer as artist) has been cleared. The Shroud is not a work of known authorship: its image's origin remains debated.

set.t: The Saviour Not Made by Hands (Mandylion of Novgorod)
set.d: second half of the 12th century (dates from the mid-12th to the early 13th century proposed)

summary: The image attached to the Wikidata item for the legendary Image of Edessa is in fact a specific, much later icon: the twelfth-century Novgorod 'Saviour Not Made by Hands'. Only the face of Christ is shown, frontal and symmetrical, with long locks falling to either side, set within a cross-inscribed halo on a gold ground. The icon follows the tradition of the Mandylion, the cloth on which Christ was believed to have imprinted his features for King Abgar of Edessa, and it is one of the oldest and most majestic icons to survive from Rus'.
facts: It is a two-sided processional icon: the reverse shows the Glorification of the Cross.

It came to the Tretyakov Gallery from the Dormition Cathedral of the Moscow Kremlin (via the State Historical Museum, 1930), but the scholar Gerold Vzdornov traced its origin to the wooden Church of the Holy Image built in Novgorod in 1191.

The legend behind the type grew over centuries: Eusebius (early 4th century) knows only a letter from Christ to Abgar; a painted portrait appears in the Doctrine of Addai (c. 400); a miraculous imprint is first described by Evagrius in 593.

links.label: Wikipedia (Russian): Спас Нерукотворный (новгородская икона XII века)

notes: The Wikidata item Q223246 describes the legendary (lost) Image of Edessa, and its location 'Şanlıurfa' refers to that relic; the image file shows the Novgorod icon (own Wikidata item Q19838804), so the entry is retitled and dated as that object. The same icon is already featured in the guided journey as 'novgorod-saviour-not-made-by-hands' (data/eras/02-byzantine-medieval.json); keep the two consistent.

set.d: probably late medieval or early Renaissance (on stylistic grounds); traditionally arrived 1508, documented from the 17th century
set.l: Santuario del Volto Santo (Capuchin friary church), Manoppello, Abruzzo, Italy
set.m: Fine, nearly transparent fabric (probably linen; byssus has been claimed), image of debated technique

summary: A small, almost transparent veil, about 17.5 by 24 cm, bearing the face of a man with open eyes, a long nose and a light beard, shown here in its silver reliquary frame in the Capuchin sanctuary at Manoppello. Local tradition holds that an unknown pilgrim brought it to the town in 1508; some modern writers have identified it with the Veil of Veronica once shown in Rome, but there is no documentary evidence connecting the cloth with Rome or with the Passion. Most researchers regard the face as an artificially made image whose style resembles works of the late Middle Ages or early Renaissance, while it remains for many pilgrims a moving image of the Holy Face.
facts: Its history — the arrival of the veil in 1508, its passing through the Leonelli and De Fabritiis families and its gift to the Capuchins — is known from the Relatione historica of Fr Donato da Bomba, based on research begun in 1640.
No samples have been allowed for laboratory analysis; a recent study concluded that linen is the most probable material, although the claim that it is woven of sea silk (byssus) is often repeated.
Pope Benedict XVI visited the sanctuary on 1 September 2006.
notes: Dating is uncertain: no technical dating exists. y=1500 reflects the stylistic judgement (late medieval / early Renaissance) and the traditional arrival in 1508. Claims of a first-century origin (H. Pfeiffer, P. Badde) are unsupported by evidence.

set.t: Our Lady of Częstochowa (The Black Madonna of Jasna Góra)
set.d: present paint layer probably mid-14th century (Italian), over an older Byzantine-type composition; repainted in Kraków 1430–1434; traditionally painted by St Luke
set.c: Unknown (Latin, probably Italian, workshop); restored in Kraków
set.l: Chapel of Our Lady, Jasna Góra Monastery, Częstochowa, Poland
set.m: Tempera on canvas laid on three lime-wood boards (122.2 × 82.2 cm)

summary: The Virgin, dark-faced and grave, holds the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures towards him, in the ancient Hodegetria ('she who shows the way') pattern; the Child raises his right hand in blessing and holds a book of the Gospels. Her blue mantle is scattered with gold fleurs-de-lis, and two parallel scars cut across her right cheek. A fifteenth-century legend says the panel was painted by St Luke on a tabletop from the house of the Holy Family; art historians instead date the present painting to the Middle Ages. Enshrined at Jasna Góra since the 1380s, it is the most venerated image in Poland, honoured as Queen of Poland.
facts: The oldest written account of its history, the fifteenth-century Translatio tabulae, describes it as the panel 'which St Luke painted with his own hands'; tradition dates its arrival at Jasna Góra to 1384.
Robbers slashed and broke the image in 1430; it was restored in Kraków in 1430–1434, and the scars on the Virgin's cheek were then deliberately incised and emphasised in memory of the attack.

Proposed dates range from the 7th to the 14th century; a 1984 analysis by Anna Różycka-Bryzek and Jerzy Gadomski found three layers — an icon-like first layer (12th–13th century), the present Italian paint layer (mid-14th century or later) and the 1430s repainting.
notes: The previous 'c' value ('Jerusalem') reproduced the St Luke legend as fact and has been replaced. Dating remains disputed (English Wikipedia reports a 6th–9th-century Byzantine original); the date given follows the 1984 technical study and the Polish scholarship summarised on pl.wikipedia. The image file is a scan from W. Kurpik, Częstochowska Hodegetria (2008), showing the panel without its votive dresses.

set.t: The Veil of Veronica (Sudarium), Wall Painting in Bonn Minster
set.l: Bonn Minster (Bonner Münster), south transept conch, beside the altar of St John the Baptist

summary: Painted on the wall of the south transept of Bonn Minster, a pale cloth carries the dark, frontal face of Christ, framed by long hair falling to either side — the 'true image' that, according to medieval legend, Christ left on the veil Veronica offered him on the way to Calvary. The painting is damaged and the face has darkened, but its stark frontality still conveys the devotional force of the Vera Icon, an image pilgrims sought in Rome and copied throughout late-medieval Europe.
scripture: Luke 23:26–31 (theme: the way to Calvary; the Veronica episode is not in the Gospels)
facts: The Veronica legend is not found in the Gospels; devotion to the Roman relic grew strongly from the 13th century, encouraged in part by Pope Innocent III, and the name 'Veronica' has been linked to the phrase vera icon, 'true image'.
Bonn Minster was largely rebuilt in late Romanesque and early Gothic style; its transept ends in polygonal conchs, in one of which this painting is found.
notes: The date c. 1320 comes from Wikidata (sourced to Bildindex der Kunst und Architektur, object 0002190240), which could not be consulted directly (bot-protected); treat as approximate. Placement from the Commons description (south conch, left of the altar of St John / Baptism of Christ).
